title: "Distributional regularisers under JEPA bottlenecks: nuisance leakage, dimension and noise on data with known factors"
author:
  - name: Ravi Kalia
date: 2026-11-08
abstract: |
  Joint-embedding predictive architectures (JEPAs) avoid representational collapse either with an
  exponential-moving-average (EMA) target or with a regulariser that pulls the embedding distribution
  towards a target law, typically an isotropic Gaussian. We ask how these regularisers — kernel Stein
  discrepancies (KSD) above all — behave when two views share a content signal but carry independent
  nuisance, and how the answer depends on two bottlenecks: the embedding dimension $d$ and Gaussian noise
  injected into the embedding. On 3DShapes, whose six generative factors are known, we split the factors
  into content ($k = 6$ probe dimensions) and nuisance, control how often nuisance is resampled between
  views, and measure nuisance leakage as the held-out $R^2$ of a linear probe. We compare eight arms
  (no regulariser, VICReg, SIGReg, sliced and full KSD, MMD, EMA, and a rank-$k$ oracle target) with
  matched tuning and {{< meta n.n_seeds >}} held-out seeds, plus a temporal tier, a CIFAR-10 tier and an
  autoencoder tier ({{< meta n.n_total_runs >}} training runs). All five hypotheses about the JEPA
  arms are refuted, and the autoencoder hypothesis is confirmed. Isotropic-Gaussian regularisers do not leak more nuisance than VICReg at content-tuned
  strength; leakage is instead governed by the regularisation weight, and rises with it for every
  regulariser. Shrinking $d$ towards $k$ reduces leakage for every arm, while injected noise never
  does. KSD with a prior matched to a non-Gaussian content law does not improve identifiability; full
  KSD towards $\mathcal N(0, I)$ has the best identifiability at every content law. In the temporal tier, EMA
  alone leaks more than sliced KSD alone. Autoencoders leak more nuisance than every JEPA arm.

# Introduction

A joint-embedding predictive architecture (JEPA) encodes two related inputs and trains a predictor to
map one embedding to the other [@assran2023self; @bardes2024revisiting]. The objective has a trivial
minimum — a constant embedding — so every JEPA needs a second ingredient. One family uses an
exponential-moving-average (EMA) target encoder with a stop-gradient, as in I-JEPA, V-JEPA and V-JEPA 2
[@assran2023self; @bardes2024revisiting; @assran2025v]. Another adds a regulariser on the batch of
embeddings: VICReg constrains variances and covariances [@bardes2022vicreg]; LeJEPA's SIGReg tests
one-dimensional projections against a standard Gaussian [@balestriero2025lejepa]; KerJEPA uses kernel
discrepancies, MMD and kernelised Stein discrepancies (KSD), sliced and unsliced
[@zimmermann2026kerjepa]. The Gaussian target is motivated by identifiability: Klindt et al. show that,
within their model class, linear identifiability of JEPA latents holds only for Gaussian latents
[@klindt2026when].

These analyses assume that the two views differ only by noise on the shared latent. Real view pairs also
differ in *nuisance*: lighting, background, pose, augmentation parameters. A distributional regulariser
asks the encoder to fill $d$ dimensions with a prescribed spread. If the content occupies fewer than $d$
dimensions, something must fill the rest, and nuisance is available. Whether this happens, and whether
the embedding dimension $d$ or an information bottleneck (noise injected into $z$) controls it, has not
been measured, because measuring it needs ground truth for both content and nuisance.

We use 3DShapes [@burgess2018shapes], a rendered dataset with a full grid of six known factors, to build
view pairs whose content is identical and whose nuisance is resampled independently with probability
$\alpha$. Linear probes on frozen embeddings then give content $R^2$, nuisance-leakage $R^2$ and an
orthogonal identifiability score, each against ground truth. This is an analysis study, not a methods
paper: all regularisers we use already exist.

**Contributions.** Relative to the 35 works we reviewed (@sec-related):

1. A controlled measurement of nuisance leakage for JEPA regularisers (VICReg, SIGReg, sliced and full
   KSD, MMD, EMA, a rank-$k$ oracle) with ground-truth nuisance whose cross-view dependence $\alpha$ is
   set by the experimenter (@sec-h1, @sec-h4).
2. A joint sweep of the dimensional bottleneck ($d$ below and above the content dimension $k$) and an
   information bottleneck (injected noise $\sigma$), with the finding that on this data the dimension,
   not the noise, limits leakage (@sec-h2).
3. A test of whether KSD with a prior matched to a non-Gaussian Euclidean content law improves
   identifiability, extending a result reported for MMD on compact manifolds [@nicollier2026beyond]; it
   does not here (@sec-h3).
4. A temporal tier comparing EMA, EMA + sliced KSD and sliced KSD on leakage when nuisance moves frame to
   frame (@sec-h5), and an autoencoder tier comparing reconstruction with prediction (@sec-h6).
5. A robustness slice showing that the regularisation weight $\lambda$, more than the target law,
   decides the leakage comparison, together with the full protocol, code and per-run results.

All five hypotheses about the JEPA arms (H1–H5), fixed before the sweep, are refuted; we report them as
such. The sixth, that autoencoders leak more than JEPAs, is confirmed.

# Related work {#sec-related}

@tbl-overlap condenses the overlap table we built from the reviewed works (35 papers, each verified
against arXiv or the venue). Three points shape our claims.

*Kernel regularisers for JEPA are not new.* KerJEPA already trains JEPAs with sliced and full KSD and MMD,
with Gaussian and IMQ kernels and Gaussian and Laplace targets [@zimmermann2026kerjepa]. SPHERE-JEPA uses
full MMD and KSD towards the uniform law on the sphere [@nicollier2026expanding], Rectified LpJEPA a
rectified generalised Gaussian [@kuang2026rectified], VISReg a variance + sliced-Wasserstein regulariser
[@wu2026visreg], and Wang and Isola a hyperspherical uniformity term for contrastive learning
[@wang2020understanding]. Our KSD and MMD arms are re-implementations of these. KSD itself comes from
goodness-of-fit testing [@liu2016a; @chwialkowski2016kernel]; the IMQ kernel controls convergence where
Gaussian kernels can fail [@gorham2017measuring]; sliced KSD is due to Gong et al. [@gong2021sliced]; and a
recent review covers Stein's method in computational statistics [@anastasiou2023steins]. Stein operators for general
multivariate and univariate densities [@mijoule2023stein; @ley2017stein], for implicit models (NP-KSD,
which we use as a metric) [@xu2022kernelised], with general operators [@xu2021generalised], and Stein
bounds for possibly singular normal targets [@reinert2009multivariate] are the background for our matched
and oracle targets.

*Matched targets and identifiability.* Beyond Gaussian Worlds shows that heat-kernel MMD towards a target
matched to the latent geometry (sphere, torus) improves linear identifiability on rendered data
[@nicollier2026beyond]. Klindt et al. vary the data law under a Gaussian target [@klindt2026when]. Our H3
is therefore a test of whether the matched-target effect carries over to KSD and to Euclidean
non-Gaussian content laws on real rendered images. Without supervision or inductive bias, disentangled
factors cannot be identified in general [@locatello2019challenging].

*Nuisance and bottlenecks.* The only reviewed works that model view-specific nuisance are contrastive
(von Kügelgen et al., who prove block-identifiability of content when style is resampled across views
[@vonkugelgen2021self]) or multi-view information bottleneck methods [@federici2020learning]. Arnez et al.
argue, in theory only, that SIGReg with fixed isotropic noise in $z$ is an exact information bottleneck
[@arnez2026sigreg]. The VAE family bottlenecks information by a KL weight [@kingma2014auto;
@higgins2017betavae; @zhao2019infovae], WAE pushes the aggregate posterior to the prior with MMD
[@tolstikhin2018wasserstein], and Stein-based VAEs use SVGD [@pu2017vae]. RankMe's effective rank
[@garrido2023rankme] is one of our metrics. Among the reviewed works, none measures nuisance leakage of a
JEPA regulariser under controlled nuisance, none sweeps $d$ and injected noise together, and none compares
EMA with KSD on leakage in a temporal JEPA; these are the cells we claim. We claim no novelty for the
regularisers, for matched targets as an idea, or for the KSD autoencoder.

# Setup {#sec-setup}

## Data and views

**3DShapes (core).** 480,000 rendered 64×64 scenes on a full grid of six factors: floor hue, wall hue and
object hue (10 values each), scale (8), shape (4) and orientation (15) [@burgess2018shapes]. We downsample
to 32×32 and store the array as a memory-mapped `uint8` file. The **content** $s$ is object shape, scale
and object hue; the **nuisance** $n$ is floor hue, wall hue and orientation. For probing, hues are encoded
as $(\cos, \sin)$ pairs and shape as a 3-dimensional regular-simplex code, so the content code is
$[\cos h, \sin h, \text{scale}, \text{simplex}(\text{shape})]$ with $k = 6$ and the nuisance code has 5
dimensions. A fixed random 10% of the factor grid is held out for probe evaluation and never used in
training.

A pair is built by drawing content once, drawing view 1's nuisance uniformly, and resampling each
nuisance factor of view 2 independently with probability $\alpha$ (@fig-views). At $\alpha = 0$ the two
views are the same image; at $\alpha = 1$ their nuisance is independent. Both views receive pixel noise
with standard deviation 0.02. The validation gates confirmed that content is identical across views at
every $\alpha$ and that at $\alpha = 1$ the largest absolute cross-view correlation of the nuisance codes
is {{< meta n.val_a1_maxcorr >}}.

![Real 3DShapes view pairs from the pair sampler at three nuisance strengths. Content (object shape,
scale, object hue) is shared; floor hue, wall hue and orientation are resampled in view 2 with
probability α.](figures/fig1_views.pdf){#fig-views width=88%}

**Content law.** To test H3, we reweight how often each object-hue and scale value is sampled: uniform
(the dataset's grid), or a discretised Gaussian or Laplace law with unit variance over a grid spanning
±2.5 sd. The images stay real; only their sampling frequencies change. Shape stays uniform.

**Temporal tier.** Clips of $T = 3$ frames from 3DShapes: content is fixed, and each nuisance factor takes
a ±1 step per frame with probability $\alpha$ (hues wrap; orientation reflects). The predictor sees the
concatenated embeddings of frames 1–2 and predicts the embedding of frame 3. We chose 3DShapes clips over
Moving MNIST [@srivastava2015unsupervised] so that the temporal tier shares the core tier's factors and
probes.

**Natural-image tier.** CIFAR-10 [@krizhevsky2009learning]: two independent augmentations of one image.
The eight augmentation parameters (crop centre, log scale, log aspect, flip, brightness, contrast,
saturation) are the nuisance, independent across views; $\alpha$ scales augmentation strength. Content is
probed through the class label on un-augmented test images.

## Objective and bottlenecks

All arms share one encoder $f_\theta$ (three 4×4 stride-2 convolutions with 16, 32 and 32 channels, then
an MLP 512 → 256 → $d$, no normalisation layers so collapse stays visible), one MLP predictor
$g_\phi$ ($d$ → 256 → $d$), Adam with learning rate $10^{-3}$ ($10^{-2}$ for the predictor), batches of
256 pairs and 2000 steps. With $z_v = f_\theta(x_v)$, the image-JEPA loss is

$$
\mathcal L = \tfrac12\big[\mathrm{MSE}(g_\phi(b_\sigma(z_1)), z_2) + \mathrm{MSE}(g_\phi(b_\sigma(z_2)), z_1)\big]
 + \lambda \cdot \tfrac12\big[R(Z_1) + R(Z_2)\big],
$$

where $R$ is the arm's regulariser on the batch $Z_v$. The two bottlenecks are:

- **dimensional:** the embedding dimension $d \in \{3, 6, 12, 24\}$, below and above $k = 6$;
- **information:** $b_\sigma(z) = z + \sigma \cdot \mathrm{sd}_B(z) \odot \xi$, $\xi \sim \mathcal N(0, I)$,
  noise on the predictor input scaled by the detached batch standard deviation, so that the
  per-dimension signal-to-noise ratio is $1/\sigma^2$ whatever the scale of $z$. Probes use the clean
  $z$. Without the scaling, the EMA and unregularised arms could escape the noise by growing $z$.

## Arms

1. **none**: $R = 0$ (collapse check).
2. **VICReg**: variance hinge plus $0.04 \times$ covariance penalty, the 25:1 ratio of
   the original paper [@bardes2022vicreg], with invariance played by the prediction loss.
3. **SIGReg**: the Epps–Pulley statistic of 256 random one-dimensional projections, computed by the
   official `lejepa` package [@balestriero2025lejepa].
4. **sliced KSD**: for random unit directions $g$, the one-dimensional IMQ Stein kernel on
   $t = g^{\mathsf{T}} z$ with projected score $g^{\mathsf{T}} \nabla \log p(z)$ (the $r = g$ variant of
   sliced KSD [@gong2021sliced]), averaged over 32 directions resampled every step.
5. **KSD**: the U-statistic
   $\widehat{\mathrm{KSD}}^2 = \frac{1}{n(n-1)}\sum_{i \neq j} u_p(z_i, z_j)$ with Langevin–Stein kernel
   $u_p(x, y) = s(x)^{\mathsf{T}} s(y)\, k(x, y) + s(x)^{\mathsf{T}} \nabla_y k + s(y)^{\mathsf{T}} \nabla_x k
   + \operatorname{tr} \nabla_x \nabla_y k$, score $s = \nabla \log p$ and IMQ base kernel
   $k(x, y) = (1 + \lVert x - y \rVert^2)^{-1/2}$ [@liu2016a; @gorham2017measuring].
6. **MMD**: unbiased MMD² against a fresh prior sample with Gaussian kernels
   $\sum_{h \in \{0.5, 1, 2\}} \exp(-\lVert x - y \rVert^2 / 2h^2 d)$.
7. **EMA**: no regulariser; the target is $\mathrm{LayerNorm}(f_\xi(x_2))$ under stop-gradient, with
   $\xi \leftarrow \tau \xi + (1 - \tau)\theta$, as in V-JEPA. Without the target LayerNorm the BYOL-style
   variant collapsed in the pilot.
8. **oracle** (diagnostic only): KSD towards the rank-$k$ target
   $\mathcal N(0, \operatorname{diag}(1_k, \varepsilon^2 1_{d-k}))$ with $\varepsilon = 0.3$, which uses the
   known $k$ and is not a practical method.

The target law $p$ is $\mathcal N(0, I_d)$ unless stated. For H3, the **matched priors** are product laws
with unit-variance coordinates: Laplace, with score $-\tanh(x/0.1)/b$ (a smoothed sign, $b = 1/\sqrt2$),
and uniform, whose score is undefined; we use the generalised-normal surrogate with shape 8 as a smooth
stand-in, and draw exact uniform samples for MMD and NP-KSD.

The temporal tier runs EMA alone (the V-JEPA recipe), EMA + sliced KSD, EMA + SIGReg, sliced KSD alone and
VICReg. The **autoencoder tier** uses the same encoder with a mirrored deconvolutional decoder and
per-image squared reconstruction error, plus either a β-weighted KL to $\mathcal N(0, I)$ (β-VAE
[@higgins2017betavae]), $\lambda$·KSD of the deterministic code batch towards the prior (KSD-AE), or
$\lambda$·MMD (MMD-AE, as WAE-MMD [@tolstikhin2018wasserstein]).

## Metrics

Probes are fitted on frozen embeddings of 10,000 training-split images and evaluated on 5,000 held-out
test-split images, both without view noise and drawn from the run's content law.

- **content $R^2$**: ridge-probe $R^2$ of the 6-dimensional content code, averaged over targets
  (CIFAR: logistic-regression class accuracy);
- **leakage $R^2$** (primary): ridge-probe $R^2$ of the 5-dimensional nuisance code (CIFAR: of the 8
  augmentation parameters); lower is better. We report kNN ($k = 10$) $R^2$ beside it, because the pilot
  found leakage that only a nonlinear probe detects;
- **identifiability**: $R^2$ of the best scaled semi-orthogonal map from centred embeddings to the
  standardised content code. It is 1 for a rotated copy of the content and
  {{< meta n.val_orth_mix >}} for a random linear mix of it (validation);
- **effective rank**: $\exp$ of the entropy of the normalised singular values of the embedding matrix
  (the quantity RankMe uses [@garrido2023rankme]); meaningless under collapse, so read with the
  embedding standard deviation;
- **Gaussianity / fit to the prior**: the sliced Epps–Pulley statistic of held-out embeddings, and an
  NP-KSD statistic [@xu2022kernelised] of 500 embeddings against the run's target law;
- **loss stability**: coefficient of variation of the loss over the last 20% of steps.

## Protocol {#sec-protocol}

**Matched tuning.** Every tuned arm gets three levels, $\lambda \times \{1/5, 1, 5\}$ around a pilot centre
(EMA: $\tau \in \{0.99, 0.996, 0.999\}$), on two validation seeds (100, 101). The level with the highest
mean validation linear content $R^2$ (CIFAR: class accuracy) is selected; leakage and identifiability are
never used, so the selection cannot favour any hypothesis. Core arms are tuned at the **base setting**
(3DShapes, $d = 12 = 2k$, $\alpha = 1$, $\sigma = 0$, uniform law) and the $d$, $\sigma$ and $\alpha$
slices reuse those levels; H3 arms are re-tuned at the Laplace law; each other tier is tuned at its own
base. @tbl-tuning lists the selections. Several land on the lowest level of their grid
(@sec-limitations).

**Held-out runs and statistics.** Each selected configuration is retrained on {{< meta n.n_seeds >}}
held-out seeds (1–5), which were not used in the pilot or in tuning: {{< meta n.n_heldout_runs >}} runs
in {{< meta n.n_heldout_configs >}} configurations, none with a non-finite loss. A λ-sensitivity slice
reruns all three tuning levels of the six λ-tuned arms at the base on the same seeds
({{< meta n.n_lam_runs >}} runs, {{< meta n.n_lam_new_runs >}} of them new). We report means with 95%
percentile-bootstrap intervals over seeds (10,000 resamples). Contrasts between arms resample each
arm's seeds independently, because different arms share no randomness; interactions are differences in
differences. With five seeds the percentile bootstrap is somewhat narrow, so we read contrasts whose
interval ends within about 0.01 of zero as weak.

**Validation gates.** Before any sweep, every regulariser was checked to be near zero on $\mathcal N(0, I)$
samples and clearly larger on collapsed or anisotropic ones (@tbl-validation); SIGReg matched `lejepa`
on the same batch and directions (relative difference {{< meta n.val_sigreg_reldiff >}}); all losses
passed float64 gradient checks and unit tests; probes recovered ground-truth factors (content $R^2$
{{< meta n.val_probe_content >}} from rotated true factors; leakage $R^2$
{{< meta n.val_probe_leak_from_content >}} from content alone); and the unregularised arm collapsed on
real images. SIGReg's statistic is $n$ times the Epps–Pulley statistic and has a positive mean under the
null.

# Results {#sec-results}

@tbl-base gives every arm at the base setting. The unregularised arm collapses (embedding standard
deviation below 0.01 in every seed of every configuration), and all regularised arms and EMA learn
content. Linear content $R^2$ stays modest because 3DShapes content is discrete (320 combinations) and no
arm is asked to arrange it linearly; kNN content $R^2$ reaches {{< meta n.shapes_ksd_content_knn_r2 >}}
for KSD.

## H1: dimension and isotropic-Gaussian targets {#sec-h1}

*H1: for $d > k$, isotropic-Gaussian regularisers increase nuisance leakage compared with VICReg and
EMA.* **Refuted under the protocol, and dependent on $\lambda$.**

At the tuned $\lambda$ and $d = 12$, the Gaussian-target arms leak less than VICReg
({{< meta n.shapes_vicreg_leak_r2_ci >}}): SIGReg {{< meta n.shapes_sigreg_leak_r2_ci >}}, sliced KSD
{{< meta n.shapes_sksd_leak_r2_ci >}}, KSD {{< meta n.shapes_ksd_leak_r2_ci >}}, MMD
{{< meta n.shapes_mmd_leak_r2_ci >}}. All {{< meta n.h1_vicreg_tot >}} Gaussian-arm − VICReg contrasts at
$d \in \{12, 24\}$ are negative with intervals that exclude zero ({{< meta n.h1_vicreg_neg >}} of
{{< meta n.h1_vicreg_tot >}}). Against EMA ({{< meta n.shapes_ema_leak_r2_ci >}}), sliced KSD, KSD and
MMD leak less at $d = 12$ and SIGReg is not different
({{< meta n.c_h1_d_12_sigreg_ema_leak_r2 >}}); at $d = 24$, SIGReg
({{< meta n.c_h1_d_24_sigreg_ema_leak_r2 >}}) and KSD ({{< meta n.c_h1_d_24_ksd_ema_leak_r2 >}}) are not
different from EMA. The one result in H1's direction is nonlinear: SIGReg's kNN leakage exceeds EMA's at
every $d$ (at $d = 12$: {{< meta n.c_h1_d_12_sigreg_ema_leak_knn_r2 >}}).

![H1: nuisance leakage and content against embedding dimension $d$ (base setting otherwise; tuned
$\lambda$). Points are means over 5 held-out seeds with 95% bootstrap intervals; the dotted line marks
$k = 6$. Leakage rises with $d$ for every arm.](figures/fig2_h1_dim.pdf){#fig-h1}

@fig-h1 shows that leakage grows with $d$ for every arm, not only the Gaussian ones. From $d = 3$ to
$d = 24$, VICReg goes from {{< meta n.shapes_vicreg_d3_leak_r2 >}} to
{{< meta n.shapes_vicreg_d24_leak_r2 >}}, SIGReg from {{< meta n.shapes_sigreg_d3_leak_r2 >}} to
{{< meta n.shapes_sigreg_d24_leak_r2 >}}, KSD from {{< meta n.shapes_ksd_d3_leak_r2 >}} to
{{< meta n.shapes_ksd_d24_leak_r2 >}} and EMA from {{< meta n.shapes_ema_d3_leak_r2 >}} to
{{< meta n.shapes_ema_d24_leak_r2 >}}; sliced KSD ({{< meta n.shapes_sksd_d24_leak_r2 >}}) and MMD
({{< meta n.shapes_mmd_d24_leak_r2 >}}) stay lowest at $d = 24$. The oracle, whose target shrinks the
$d - k$ extra directions to standard deviation 0.3, still leaks heavily for $d > k$
({{< meta n.shapes_oracle_leak_r2 >}} at $d = 12$, {{< meta n.shapes_oracle_d24_leak_r2 >}} at
$d = 24$): linear probes are scale-invariant, so shrinking a direction does not remove the nuisance it
carries. At $d = 3$, EMA collapsed in {{< meta n.shapes_ema_d3_collapsed >}} seeds and MMD in
{{< meta n.shapes_mmd_d3_collapsed >}}, so those two points mix collapsed and non-collapsed runs.

**The weight $\lambda$ decides the comparison.** Tuning on validation seeds already showed leakage
tracking $\lambda$, so we reran all three tuning levels on the held-out seeds (@fig-lambda). For every
regulariser, VICReg included, the highest level leaks more than the lowest, with intervals excluding zero
({{< meta n.lam_pos >}} of {{< meta n.lam_tot >}}); for KSD the difference is
{{< meta n.c_h1_lam_ksd_l_5_l_0_2_leak_r2 >}} and for VICReg
{{< meta n.c_h1_lam_vicreg_l_25_l_1_leak_r2 >}}. At five times its content-optimal level, each
Gaussian-target arm leaks more than VICReg's least-leaky level ({{< meta n.lam_vicreg_l1_leak_r2_ci >}});
for KSD at $\lambda = 1$ the gap is {{< meta n.c_h1_lam_ksd_l_1_vicreg_l_1_its_least_leaky_level_leak_r2 >}},
and against EMA {{< meta n.c_h1_lam_ksd_l_1_ema_leak_r2 >}}. Because our selection rule maximises
content $R^2$ and content $R^2$ falls with $\lambda$, it picks low-leakage levels. The verdict on H1 is
therefore a statement about content-tuned regularisers; under stronger distributional pressure the
Gaussian arms do leak more than VICReg and EMA. More pressure buys leakage for every regulariser, so the
effect is not specific to isotropic-Gaussian targets.

![λ sensitivity at the base setting on held-out seeds: leakage and content at each arm's three tuning
levels, plotted against λ divided by the tuned λ. The grey band is EMA's 95% interval.
](figures/fig3_lambda.pdf){#fig-lambda width=90%}

## H2: dimensional against information bottleneck {#sec-h2}

*H2: the information bottleneck ($\sigma$) reduces leakage where the dimensional one ($d$) does not.*
**Refuted; the opposite holds.**

Narrowing $d$ reduces linear leakage for all six arms (σ = 0, $d = 6$ against $d = 24$, intervals excluding
zero): for example EMA {{< meta n.c_h2_ema_s_0_d_6_d_24_leak_r2 >}}, KSD
{{< meta n.c_h2_ksd_s_0_d_6_d_24_leak_r2 >}} and MMD {{< meta n.c_h2_mmd_s_0_d_6_d_24_leak_r2 >}}.
Injected noise never reduces linear leakage (@fig-sigma). At σ = 1 against σ = 0, leakage rises for EMA,
SIGReg, sliced KSD, KSD and MMD at both $d$, for example KSD at $d = 12$
{{< meta n.c_h2_ksd_d_12_s_1_0_s_0_leak_r2 >}} and MMD {{< meta n.c_h2_mmd_d_12_s_1_0_s_0_leak_r2 >}};
VICReg is unchanged ({{< meta n.c_h2_vicreg_d_12_s_1_0_s_0_leak_r2 >}}). Noise also lowers content $R^2$
for every arm. The only reduction is EMA's kNN leakage
({{< meta n.c_h2_ema_d_12_s_1_0_s_0_leak_knn_r2 >}} at $d = 12$), and it comes with a larger loss of kNN
content ({{< meta n.shapes_ema_content_knn_r2 >}} → {{< meta n.shapes_ema_s1_content_knn_r2 >}}): the
embedding degrades rather than filtering nuisance. EMA's loss is also unstable under noise (coefficient of
variation of the loss {{< meta n.shapes_ema_s05_loss_cv_last20 >}} at σ = 0.5 and
{{< meta n.shapes_ema_s1_loss_cv_last20 >}} at σ = 1 for $d = 12$, against
{{< meta n.shapes_ema_loss_cv_last20 >}} without noise).

![H2: leakage and content against injected noise σ at $d = 12$ and $d = 24$ (α = 1, uniform law,
tuned λ). Noise never lowers linear leakage and lowers content for every arm.
](figures/fig4_h2_sigma.pdf){#fig-sigma}

## H3: matched priors under non-Gaussian content laws {#sec-h3}

*H3: with non-Gaussian content laws, KSD with a matched prior beats Gaussian-target regularisers on
identifiability.* **Refuted.**

Under the uniform law, matched-uniform KSD
({{< meta n.shapes_ksd_prioruniform_ident_orth_r2_ci >}}) is not different from KSD towards
$\mathcal N(0, I)$ ({{< meta n.shapes_ksd_ident_orth_r2_ci >}}; difference
{{< meta n.c_h3_law_uniform_ksd_matched_ksd_ident_orth_r2 >}}). It beats SIGReg, sliced KSD, MMD and the
oracle, but so does Gaussian-target KSD: the advantage belongs to full KSD, not to the matched prior.
Under the Laplace law, matched-Laplace KSD ({{< meta n.shapes_ksd_lawlaplace_priorlaplace_ident_orth_r2_ci >}})
is far below Gaussian-target KSD ({{< meta n.shapes_ksd_lawlaplace_ident_orth_r2_ci >}}; difference
{{< meta n.c_h3_law_laplace_ksd_matched_ksd_ident_orth_r2 >}}) and also below SIGReg
({{< meta n.c_h3_law_laplace_ksd_matched_sigreg_ident_orth_r2 >}}). Matched sliced KSD is below every
Gaussian-target arm at both laws (@fig-law, @tbl-h3). Full KSD towards $\mathcal N(0, I)$ has the best
identifiability at every law, and its highest value is under the Laplace law.

![H3: orthogonal identifiability by content law (d = 12). Filled markers: Gaussian targets; open
markers: KSD and sliced KSD with a prior matched to the content law (at the Gaussian law the matched
prior is $\mathcal N(0, I)$).](figures/fig5_h3_law.pdf){#fig-law width=86%}

Three caveats limit this verdict. Laplace-target KSD has little power at batch size 256: in validation it
scored {{< meta n.val_ksd_lap_exact >}} on an exact Laplace sample and {{< meta n.val_ksd_lap_gauss >}}
on a Gaussian one (uniform target: {{< meta n.val_ksd_unif_exact >}} against
{{< meta n.val_ksd_unif_gauss >}}). The trained matched-Laplace embeddings do not reach their prior
(NP-KSD {{< meta n.shapes_ksd_lawlaplace_priorlaplace_npksd_prior >}} for KSD and
{{< meta n.shapes_sksd_lawlaplace_priorlaplace_npksd_prior >}} for sliced KSD, against
{{< meta n.shapes_ksd_lawlaplace_npksd_prior >}} for Gaussian-target KSD towards its own target). And the
matched prior acts on all $d = 12$ coordinates while the law changes only two content factors.

{{< include _generated/tab_h3.md >}}

: H3: identifiability (orthogonal $R^2$) by content law and target; mean [95% CI] over 5 held-out seeds.
{#tbl-h3}

## H4: EMA under nuisance {#sec-h4}

*H4: EMA/stop-gradient behaves qualitatively differently from distributional regularisers under
nuisance.* **Refuted for the leakage response; its geometry does differ.**

Raising $\alpha$ from 0 to 1 lowers leakage or leaves it unchanged for every arm and raises content
(@fig-alpha): EMA {{< meta n.c_h4_ema_a_1_a_0_leak_r2 >}}, KSD {{< meta n.c_h4_ksd_a_1_a_0_leak_r2 >}},
sliced KSD {{< meta n.c_h4_sliced_ksd_a_1_a_0_leak_r2 >}}, MMD {{< meta n.c_h4_mmd_a_1_a_0_leak_r2 >}},
SIGReg {{< meta n.c_h4_sigreg_a_1_a_0_leak_r2 >}}, VICReg {{< meta n.c_h4_vicreg_a_1_a_0_leak_r2 >}}.
In differences of differences, EMA's response is not different from KSD's
({{< meta n.c_h4_interaction_ema_a1_a0_ksd_a1_a0_leak_r2 >}}) or sliced KSD's
({{< meta n.c_h4_interaction_ema_a1_a0_sliced_ksd_a1_a0_leak_r2 >}}), and EMA's drop is larger than VICReg's
({{< meta n.c_h4_interaction_ema_a1_a0_vicreg_a1_a0_leak_r2 >}}), SIGReg's and MMD's. EMA sits inside the
range of the regularisers. The difference is at the middle level and in geometry: at α = 0.5 EMA leaks
{{< meta n.shapes_ema_a05_leak_r2 >}} while sliced KSD, KSD and MMD leak
{{< meta n.shapes_sksd_a05_leak_r2 >}}, {{< meta n.shapes_ksd_a05_leak_r2 >}} and
{{< meta n.shapes_mmd_a05_leak_r2 >}}; and at α = 1 EMA's embedding has standard deviation
{{< meta n.shapes_ema_emb_std_mean >}} and effective rank {{< meta n.shapes_ema_eff_rank >}}, against
{{< meta n.shapes_sksd_eff_rank >}}–{{< meta n.shapes_sigreg_eff_rank >}} for the regularisers.

![H4: leakage and content against nuisance strength α (d = 12, σ = 0). At α = 0 the two views are the
same image, so nuisance is fully predictable from the other view.](figures/fig6_h4_alpha.pdf){#fig-alpha}

## H5: temporal tier {#sec-h5}

*H5: with nuisance that moves over time, EMA + stop-gradient alone leaks less nuisance than any
distributional regulariser alone, and adding sliced KSD to EMA leaves leakage unchanged within the CIs.*
**Refuted on both parts** (@tbl-temporal, @fig-h5h6 left).

EMA alone leaks more than sliced KSD alone ({{< meta n.c_h5_ema_sliced_ksd_alone_leak_r2 >}}) and is not
different from VICReg ({{< meta n.c_h5_ema_vicreg_alone_leak_r2 >}}; on kNN leakage EMA is higher,
{{< meta n.c_h5_ema_vicreg_alone_leak_knn_r2 >}}). Adding sliced KSD to EMA raises leakage
({{< meta n.c_h5_emapsksd_ema_leak_r2 >}}); adding SIGReg gives
{{< meta n.c_h5_emapsigreg_ema_leak_r2 >}}. Leakage is high for every temporal arm because the target
frame's nuisance is one ±1 step from the context, so it is predictable from the context and an encoder
that keeps it lowers the prediction loss.

## H6: autoencoders against JEPA {#sec-h6}

*H6: at matched $d$, reconstruction-based models leak more nuisance than every JEPA arm.* **Confirmed.**
All {{< meta n.h6_tot_leak_r2 >}} contrasts (three autoencoders × seven JEPA arms, $d = 12$, linear
leakage) are positive with intervals excluding zero ({{< meta n.h6_pos_leak_r2 >}} of
{{< meta n.h6_tot_leak_r2 >}}), and so are {{< meta n.h6_pos_leak_knn_r2 >}} of
{{< meta n.h6_tot_leak_knn_r2 >}} kNN contrasts (@tbl-vae, @fig-h5h6 right). The smallest gap is β-VAE
against VICReg, {{< meta n.c_h6_betavae_ae_jepa_vicreg_leak_r2 >}}. H3's matched-prior question carries
over as a null-to-negative result: under the Laplace law, the Laplace-prior KSD autoencoder has lower
identifiability than the Gaussian-prior one
({{< meta n.c_h6_ksd_ae_laplace_law_matched_laplace_prior_gaussian_prior_ident_orth_r2 >}}) and the same
content $R^2$ ({{< meta n.c_h6_ksd_ae_laplace_law_matched_laplace_prior_gaussian_prior_content_r2 >}}).

## Natural images (CIFAR-10)

The CIFAR-10 tier carries no hypothesis (@tbl-cifar). Every regularised arm reaches similar class
accuracy, KSD highest ({{< meta n.cifar_ksd_class_acc_ci >}}) and EMA lowest of the trained arms
({{< meta n.cifar_ema_class_acc_ci >}}); the unregularised arm collapses. Linear leakage of the
augmentation parameters is small for every arm ({{< meta n.cifar_ksd_leak_r2 >}} to
{{< meta n.cifar_ema_leak_r2 >}}, EMA highest); Gaussian-target arms differ from VICReg by at most a few
hundredths. With augmentation-defined nuisance and the class as content, the isotropic regularisers do not
leak nuisance linearly to any notable degree. The oracle is omitted here because CIFAR has no known $k$.

# Discussion: dimensional against information bottleneck {#sec-discussion}

The results fit one reading, which we offer as an interpretation rather than a tested claim. A
distributional regulariser asks for $d$ dimensions of spread. When the shared content provides fewer
($d > k$), the cheapest way to meet the demand is to spend the spare directions on whatever else varies
in the image, and on 3DShapes that is the nuisance. Three manipulations change how hard the demand
presses, and for the distributional regularisers all three move leakage the way this reading predicts: larger $d$ leaves more spare directions
(@fig-h1); larger $\lambda$ weights the demand more heavily (@fig-lambda); and the scaled noise of H2
makes every direction less useful for prediction, which weakens the pull of the prediction loss
towards content relative to the regulariser (@fig-sigma). Only shrinking $d$ removes room for nuisance. EMA has no explicit demand, and its
embedding stays low-rank, but it still leaks once $d$ exceeds $k$: in a predictive objective without a
spread constraint nothing pushes nuisance out of the spare directions either.

On this reading the dimensional bottleneck is a filter and the information bottleneck, as we implemented
it, is not. The noise here is scaled to the batch standard deviation of each coordinate, so the encoder
cannot raise the signal-to-noise ratio of content relative to nuisance by rescaling; an information
bottleneck that charges per bit of $I(z; x)$, such as a learned-variance KL term, or noise fixed in
absolute scale as in the analysis of Arnez et al. [@arnez2026sigreg], might behave differently. We did not
test those. A second qualification: the predictor reads the noisy $z$ while the probes read the clean
$z$, so the noise can also change what the encoder writes into dimensions the predictor learns to ignore.

The H3 result runs against the motivation for matched targets. Two explanations are compatible with our
data and we cannot separate them: KSD towards a Laplace target has little power at our batch size, so
the matched arm receives a weak and noisy training signal; and the matched prior constrains all twelve
coordinates while only two content factors follow the law. That full KSD towards $\mathcal N(0, I)$ is
best at every law agrees with KerJEPA's use of full KSD [@zimmermann2026kerjepa] and suggests that, at
this scale, the quality of the training signal matters more than the shape of the target.

Finally, the λ-sensitivity slice is the result we would most want a practitioner to see. A study that
fixed $\lambda$ for each regulariser at a conventional value could reach the opposite verdict on H1 from
ours, and both would be correct for their $\lambda$. Leakage comparisons between regularisers are only
meaningful together with the rule that set their strengths.

# Limitations {#sec-limitations}

- **Rendered core data.** 3DShapes is rendered, with a small discrete factor grid; content $R^2$ is
  bounded by its discreteness, and its nuisance (colours, orientation) is simpler than real nuisance.
- **Augmentation-defined nuisance.** On CIFAR-10 the nuisance is our augmentation, not a property of the
  scene, so its leakage measures invariance to our own transformations.
- **Small scale.** A three-layer encoder at 32×32, 2000 steps and $d \le 24$. All runs trained on one
  laptop GPU, six at a time ({{< meta n.run_hours >}} hours of summed per-run training and evaluation time). Larger encoders and
  longer training may change every effect.
- **Tuning.** λ was tuned only at the base setting and reused across $d$, σ and α, so part of the $d$ and
  σ effects may come from a λ that is no longer optimal there. Several selected levels sit at the lowest
  end of their grid (sliced KSD, KSD, matched-uniform KSD; SIGReg and oracle at the Laplace law; several
  autoencoders), so lower λ might score higher still. The validation selection is noisy: SIGReg's
  held-out content $R^2$ is higher at λ = 0.01 ({{< meta n.lam_sigreg_l001_content_r2 >}}) than at the
  selected 0.05 ({{< meta n.lam_sigreg_l005_content_r2 >}}).
- **Statistics.** Five seeds per configuration, unpaired across arms, with percentile-bootstrap
  intervals that are somewhat narrow at $n = 5$. The EMA arm is the least stable across seeds.
- **The oracle** uses the true content dimension and is a diagnostic only.
- **One information bottleneck** (batch-scaled noise on the predictor input) among several possible.
- **Literature coverage.** Novelty claims are relative to 35 reviewed works found by a targeted search;
  2026 preprints are not exhaustively covered.

# Future work

The natural next steps are data with richer nuisance and known factors — Causal3DIdent
[@vonkugelgen2021self] and MPI3D-real — and natural images with a held-out nuisance label, such as
ImageNette with recorded augmentation; real video for the temporal tier; an information bottleneck with a
learned rate; and λ tuned at every point of the $d$ and σ slices.

# Reproducibility statement

All code, configurations and per-run results are in the study repository. `REPRODUCE.md` gives the
exact commands, seeds, environment and hardware. Every run is keyed by a hash of its full configuration;
the tables in `results/` are generated by `stein.analyze`, and every number, table and figure in this
paper is generated from them by `stein.report` and inserted at render time — no number in the text is
typed by hand. Seeds are fixed. As a check, we retrained the {{< meta n.repro_n >}} temporal-tier runs
from scratch in an empty run cache on the same machine: {{< meta n.repro_bitwise >}} of
{{< meta n.repro_n >}} reproduced every metric bitwise. MPS kernels are not guaranteed to be
deterministic across hardware or software versions, so reruns elsewhere may differ slightly. The study (experiments, analysis and this
draft) was carried out by an AI agent (Claude) under a protocol and hypotheses fixed before the
sweep, with its own validation gates.
